Long post incoming.

You're 15. I know that feels like you've been around long enough to know life, but you wouldn't feel that way in 5 years, let alone 20. And those years go by fast. I've never known a 15 year old who was living life with any of the same perspectives on life that they have as an adult. And I've known a few adults who were grateful that they didn't give into the existential despair that often comes with teenage years by committing suicide.

If you're gonna do it, you're gonna do it, and obviously I can't stop you. But I'd like to give you some things to think about before you do, if you'd be willing to consider them.

First, let's talk about that existential despair. I think it is actually a very reasonable reaction. At 15, most of your perspective of life has been defined by family, by the public education system, by mass media, and by peers who have had their lives shaped by those same forces. The public education system is an indoctrination machine, generally run by the most mediocre of adults, with the intent of impressing upon you a continually failed ideology (and an actual result of preparing you to be a cog in a the faceless machine of corporate work environments). Mass media is a set of businesses, that only survive by trying to constantly spike and depress your dopamine responses so that you become addicted to giving them attention. It cannot matter to them if you are healthy and well-informed about the world, because making that a priority would put them out of business. They generally give people a terrible and false view of the world, strip them of all meaningful identity, and convince them to constantly try to escape life in one way or another. Families are frequently composed of broken beings who no longer know how to have healthy relationships and teach people how to develop meaning and purpose, because they've been living in that same system for a few generations now. And, of course, your peers are generally in the same boat (although many of them will pretend otherwise for status, and a few of them have been raised in the rare, healthy environment).

You probably haven't been taught self-discipline, your brain chemistry and general health is probably in shambles, you are probably surrounded by people who do more to destroy you than build you up, you probably have no meaningful identity groups, and you probably have some nebulous and unarticulated life philosophy that gives you no aims to feel like striving for. Despair, or a defensive strategy of emotional numbness, are the most reasonable reactions to being raised in the modern world, as far as I can tell.

But the perspective of the modern person - especially the modern young adult - is based on falsehoods. You feel alone because you have never been taught how to articulate your feelings in a clear and true manner, so that other people might relate. You feel alone because other people commonly filter their feelings through their desires to manipulate other's actions or beliefs, so that you never see who they are and thus cannot relate to them on a deep level. You feel alone because you do not share any higher aims with a people who might function like a tribe to you, because you have not yet discovered any higher aims. You feel alone because you see yourself as your highest priority - much like a finger only seeing itself and not understanding its purpose as a member of a complete body.

And, your view of the world is tinged with the negative feelings that are inherent to poor health, physical and mental. You probably won't be conscious of this, as most people think that they perceive the world directly, but people generally just see a reflection of the world distorted by the bent and cracked mirror of the inside of their own mind.

So, this is what I'd ask you to contemplate:

I'd like you to picture yourself, surrounded by people who are as smart as you are, who speak with you honestly, who work to make sure you are the best and strongest and most fulfilled person you can be - and who expect and demand that you do the same for them. I'd like you to picture yourself as someone who really believes that you can do the same for them. I'd like you to picture yourself and these people working to achieve a goal. This is a large and difficult goal that will make life better for the whole group in some significant way. But, as large and difficult as it is, you are all making progress on it. And you play a key role in this goal - it will be much harder without you. You are free, you can do as you want and nobody can stop you since you own your own life; as an adult you have your own home and schedule and make your own decisions. But you want to bind yourself to these expectations, and you do. You want to bind yourself to this group, and help protect it against any opposing interests of people outside this group. You can tell yourself what to do, and you are self-disciplined enough that you'll obey yourself. And you feel energetic, strong, calm, and focused while doing it.

This is the natural state of being human. This is the natural state of tribal life in a wild world. This is the environment we are evolved to function most efficiently in. This is what satisfies us on a deep level. It is increasingly uncommon in the modern world, and the social narrative of modern society pretends it doesn't exist. But it is not impossible; in fact, it happens somewhat regularly. It just doesn't get modeled in movies or television shows or video games very well, and so it seems non-existent.

So, if a person decides they want to get there, how do they get there? Here's a list of suggestions I'd give to someone who'd want to try this life out.

  • First and foremost, speak honestly. This obviously means that you shouldn't tell false stories, but it also means that you shouldn't speak with the intention of making people see you in a particular way or do a particular thing for you. You still would have interests that you want other people to help you with, but you do this by clearly stating your intentions, not by trying to manipulate. You don't speak with the purpose of increasing your status in another person's eyes. If you cannot say what is completely true, you simply remain silent, or state that you don't wish to speak on it. But if something needs to be said, you say it. If a person does this for long enough, they start to gather around themselves like-minded people who appreciate the truth, and who will speak it to you also. Groups clearly speaking the truth to each other, and who appreciate hearing the truth from each other, will develop common interests and work efficiently toward common goals with loyalty.

  • Pick a hobby that requires you to create something, and requires you to develop skills in order to create it well. This could be drawing, or computer coding, or woodworking, or anything like that. You'll suck when you start. Be okay with that, because that is necessary. Work on it when you'd normally be mindlessly sitting in front of a screen, or masturbating/fucking, or doing whatever you do with your free time that isn't making you happy and better in the long-run. Keep a journal of what you're learning, and so you can clearly see how you're improving.

  • Get 8 hours of sleep (or lay in bed trying to sleep for 8 hours) every night. Don't have any screens on during this time. Wake up around the same time every day. People generally don't know how inconsistent sleep patterns screw with your neurochemistry and can easily make you depressed.

  • Get sunlight and fresh air for at least 20 minutes every day; more if you can manage it. We're built to be outside in nature, and being trapped in walls for so long screws with our ability to realize how connected we are to everything else.

  • Quit eating/drinking so much junk. Eat more vegetables, drink more water. Eat less sugar, less refined grains (stuff made with white flour), and less fried foods. You are messing up your hormone balance and making yourself less energetic with the modern diet. But make sure to eat enough. If you find that (like many people in the modern world) you are actually addicted to certain types of junk food and you can't make yourself stop until you've developed self-discipline, then just keep adding on healthy food and water to what you're already eating for now.

  • Find time, at least once a week, to spend time with people who share your hobby and are trying to develop the same skills as you. If you can't find this at first, keep looking, but spend time with people who support your growth and want to talk about your hobby. Strive to do it at least once a week.

  • Stop complaining. This doesn't mean you can't talk about the things that are wrong in your life, because you should. But you should speak about it with the people who can help you fix it, with the intention of figuring out how to fix it. Don't just complain to them. And don't complain in your head about how terrible your life or the world is - this accomplishes nothing, but makes sure that you view the world in the reflections of a very dark mirror of your mind. Stop spending time with people who complain all the time. Just cut them out of your life as much as you can.

(continued...)

  • Get some physical movement everyday. Exercise if you can, but even just going for walks and stretching will help. Even if you don't get in "great shape" from what you're doing, it's really about creating the hormonal and neurochemical balance that help you see life clearly and keep you out of depression, so you can make choices for yourself.

  • If ever you don't know what to do, or feel like life is meaningless, picture the scenario I asked you to picture above. Aim yourself at actions that bring you closer to that. Aim yourself away from situations that lead you further away from that.

  • Understand that happiness is not the aim of life. Happiness is a byproduct of successfully and skillfully overcoming struggles and challenges. If you aim for happiness as your highest priority, you will never achieve it for very long. If you aim for strength, truth, and development in overcoming hardships, happiness and satisfaction will frequently flow in without you even trying for it.

If a person were to do these things, they'd start down a path to feel much more connected, much more purposeful, much more driven, and much more satisfied in life than the average person in the modern world. It has worked for me, and I've seen it work for people around me - even those who were once drowning in the black nothingness of the void of modern life. And, when the time comes, you'll start to see that life has a purpose - one that can't easily be described in mere text, but is only known through direct experience. That is why I'd suggest it.

But, that is only if you'd prefer things to be better in the way I've described. It is your life, and if you want to end it, that is your choice to make. I hope you choose what's right for you.

Good luck, my friend.
